standards.applicability: Applies to accounting and financial reporting for all transactions involving Wa'ad, Khiyar or Tahawwut arrangements carried out under Shari'ah principles and rules by Islamic financial institutions (paras 1-2); to be read together with definitions/Shari'ah principles in the listed AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards and with the Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting (unnumbered note preceding Preface); no explicit exclusions stated (absent).
standards.structure: Preface (PR1-PR3); Introduction - Overview, Rationale for issuing this standard (IN1-IN7); Objective of the standard (para 1); Scope (para 2); Definitions (para 3, a-j incl. binding/non-binding Wa'ad); Types and classification of Wa'ad, Khiyar and Tahawwut arrangements (para 4, ancillary vs product); Accounting for ancillary Wa'ad or Khiyar - Recognition and measurement (paras 5-7), Presentation and disclosure (paras 8-10); Accounting for product Wa'ad or Khiyar - Accounting for obligations (Initial recognition paras 11-12, Subsequent measurement para 13, Derecognition paras 14-15, Presentation and disclosure para 16), Accounting for rights (Initial recognition paras 17-18, Subsequent measurement para 19, Derecognition paras 20-21, Presentation and disclosure para 22), Multiple Wa'ad and Khiyar arrangements (para 23), Assessment of the probability of the flow of economic resources (para 24), Hamish Jiddiyyah and Arboun (paras 25-27); Accounting for Tahawwut (hedging) arrangements (paras 28-34, hedging instrument/hedged item designation, qualifying criteria, fair value hedges, cash flow hedges, discontinuation, recycling); Effective date (para 35); Appendix A: Adoption of the standard (Members of the board, Reservation, Working group members, Executive team); Appendix B: Basis for conclusions (BC1-BC13); Appendix C: Brief history of the preparation of the standard (H1-H10).
key_points: Standard prescribes accounting and reporting principles for recognition, measurement and disclosure of Shari'ah-compliant Wa'ad (promise), Khiyar (option) and Tahawwut (hedging) arrangements for Islamic financial institutions (para 1).
Scope covers all transactions involving Wa'ad, Khiyar or Tahawwut arrangements carried out under Shari'ah principles and rules (para 2).

Wa'ad is a unilateral undertaking (constructive obligation) understood to be binding in Shari'ah on the promisor unless a legitimate Shari'ah excuse prevents fulfillment; classified as binding Wa'ad (pending on a cause where the promisee has incurred costs, or expressly made binding by the promisor) or non-binding Wa'ad (para 3.j, i-ii).

Khiyar (option) is an expressed or implied option within a sale, Ijarah or other contract allowing one party to unilaterally nullify, revoke, or materially amend the contract; Tahawwut (hedging) arrangement mitigates risk of unfavorable future fair value changes or cash flow differentials via a Wa'ad or Khiyar (or series thereof) for a stipulated period (para 3.e, 3.i).

Other definitions: Control = substantially all risks/rewards of ownership via exposure to variable returns and ability to affect those returns; Fair value = price received to sell an asset/paid to transfer a liability between market participants at the measurement date; Onerous contract or commitment = unavoidable costs exceed expected economic benefits; Promisor/Promisee defined, promisee may incur cost by reason of the promise (para 3.b, 3.c, 3.f, 3.g-h).

Arboun = security-cum-advance sale payment, forfeitable by the seller on the buyer's revocation of purchase within an agreed period; Hamish Jiddiyyah = a security deposit for fulfillment of a contract/promise, of which only actual damages may be forfeited, applying only to the pre-contracting period and not usable throughout the contract term (para 3.a, 3.d).

Arrangements are classified as ancillary Wa'ad or Khiyar (tied to the structure of a Shari'ah-compliant arrangement, e.g. a Murabaha purchase-orderer's promise or a post-term purchase promise in Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, or the option of inspection) or product Wa'ad or Khiyar (stand-alone, e.g. an FX forward promise, a cancellation option with Arboun, a Shari'ah-compliant alternative to a repurchase (RePO) transaction, or a Tahawwut arrangement) (para 4.a-b).

An ancillary Wa'ad or Khiyar by itself gives rise to no asset or liability; the institution assesses each reporting period whether it has become an onerous contract or commitment, accounted per FAS 30 "Impairment, Credit Losses and Onerous Commitments" (paras 5-7).

Ancillary Wa'ad or Khiyar: qualitative disclosure of nature required; significant outstanding arrangements disclosed under contingent liabilities/commitments (and assets, if applicable) per FAS 1; onerous items presented/disclosed per FAS 30 (paras 8-10).

Product Wa'ad or Khiyar obligation recognition: a recognised constructive obligation arises when it is 'more likely than not' that economic resources will flow out and the amount is reliably measurable, initially recorded at a reasonable fair value estimate with corresponding loss to the statement of income (paras 11-12).

Product Wa'ad or Khiyar right recognition: a recognised constructive right arises only when it is 'highly probable' that resources will flow to the institution, a legal or constructive obligation exists for that flow, and the amount is reliably measurable, recorded at a reasonable fair value estimate of the receivable (paras 17-18).

Subsequent measurement: carrying amounts of the recognised constructive obligation and recognised constructive right are reviewed each reporting period with gains/losses taken to the statement of income, except amounts pertaining to a Tahawwut arrangement, accounted per paras 28-34 (paras 13, 19).

Derecognition: the obligation is derecognised on extinguishment, expiry/cancellation, or ceasing to meet the para 11 recognition criteria; the right is derecognised on expiry of contractual rights or ceasing to meet the para 17 criteria; gains/losses on derecognition go to the statement of income (paras 14-15, 20-21).

Minimum disclosures include accounting policies/judgments and estimates, carrying amounts and movements of recognised obligations/rights, the amount of gain or loss recognised in income (segregating initial recognition from subsequent reassessment effects for rights), and the gain or loss on a Tahawwut (hedge) relationship attributed to the hedged item (paras 16, 22).

Multiple Wa'ad and Khiyar arrangements - bilateral, parallel, multi-lateral, or series arrangements by independent parties - are accounted for by applying the standard's requirements to each individual Wa'ad or Khiyar separately (para 23).

Probability-of-flow assessment factors (inter-alia): the legal and regulatory environment; whether the Wa'ad or Khiyar has significant economic incentive for the counterparty; existence of collateral, security, guarantee, margin or variation margin held/placed; industry practice in similar situations; costs incurred in good faith by the counterparty; and public expectation/trust in the institution as an upholder of Shari'ah (para 24.a-f).

Hamish Jiddiyyah or Arboun received or paid constitutes an asset or liability, accounted per the relevant AAOIFI FAS; it is not netted off against the recognised constructive obligation/right absent a legally enforceable netting right; Arboun paid may be adjusted against the sale consideration once the sale is consummated (paras 25-27).

Hedge designation requires a hedged item (an asset, liability, firm commitment, or highly probable forecast transaction exposed to fair value or cash flow risk and designated as hedged) and a hedging instrument (a designated Wa'ad or Khiyar, made to a party external to the institution, expected to offset that risk) (para 28.a-b).

A hedging relationship qualifies for hedge accounting only where formally documented per the institution's risk management objectives and an economic relationship exists between the hedging instrument and the hedged item, and is accounted for only when adequately documented, expected effective, cash-flow exposure is probable (cash flow hedges), effectiveness is reliably measurable, and ongoing high effectiveness is assessed each period (paras 29-30).

Fair value hedge accounting: the gain or loss from remeasuring the hedging instrument at fair value is recognised in the statement of income; the gain or loss on the hedged item adjusts its carrying amount and is also recognised in the statement of income (para 31.a-b).

Cash flow hedge accounting: the effective portion of the gain or loss on the hedging instrument is recognised in equity (owners' equity and quasi-equity); the ineffective portion is recognised in the statement of income (para 32.a-b).

Hedge accounting is discontinued when the hedging instrument expires, is settled, terminated or exercised (with exceptions for mandated clearing-counterparty replacement or documented replacement/renewal/rollover strategies), when the hedge no longer meets the para 29 qualifying criteria, or when the institution revokes the hedge designation (para 33.a-c, i-ii).

For cash flow hedges other than those in para 32, amounts previously recognised in equity are recycled to the statement of income in the same period(s) the hedged forecast cash flows affect income; the standard is effective for financial statements beginning on or after 1 January 2022, with earlier application permitted (paras 34-35).

divergence_evidence.position: AAOIFI: Wa'ad (promise) is a unilateral undertaking (constructive obligation) assumed by a party, understood to be binding in Shari'ah on the individual who makes it unless a legitimate excuse under Shari'ah arises and prevents its fulfillment; classified as binding Wa'ad (becomes binding by virtue of juristic rules if pending on a cause and the promisee has incurred costs by reason of the promise, or by the promisor expressly making it binding on itself) or non-binding Wa'ad (any Wa'ad other than a binding promise) (para 3.j)

standards.title: AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standard (FAS) 39 "Financial Reporting for Zakah"
standards.effective_date: 2023-01-01, for financial periods beginning on or after this date; early adoption permitted (Effective date)

standards.applicability: Applies to an institution regarding recognition, presentation and disclosure of Zakah attributable to relevant stakeholders, on both consolidated and separate/stand-alone financial statements (Scope); does not prescribe the method for determining the Zakah base or measuring Zakah due, which institutions must obtain from SS 35 "Zakah", regulatory requirements, or their Shari'ah supervisory board (Scope); excludes Zakah on agricultural produce and other non-annual produce, for which the institution develops its own accounting policy and reconciliation disclosures (Scope); creditors, including current account depositors, are not treated as participatory stakeholders and their balances are outside scope (BC12).
term_names: Institutions not obliged to pay Zakah
standards.structure: Preface (PR1-PR4); Introduction - Overview, Rationale for issuing this standard, Significant changes from previous standard (IN1-IN6); Objective of the standard; Scope; Definitions (a-j); Institutions obliged to pay Zakah - Recognition of Zakah due and corresponding liability (Recognition of current Zakah due as an expense, Recognition of Zakah as adjustment to equity, Recognition of Zakah liability); Institutions not obliged to pay Zakah; Presentation and disclosure requirements (a-l) incl. Zakah fund; Effective date; Amendments to other standards; Appendix A: Adoption of the standard (Members of the board, Reservation, Working group members, Executive team); Appendix B(i) and B(ii): Illustrative disclosure of calculation and attribution of Zakah; Appendix C: Illustrative disclosure for sources and application of Zakah; Appendix D: Basis for conclusions (BC1-BC17); Appendix E: Brief history of the preparation of the standard (H1-H16).
key_points: Standard establishes principles of financial reporting for Zakah attributable to different stakeholders of an Islamic financial institution (Objective of the standard).

Standard does not prescribe the method for determining the Zakah base or measuring Zakah due for a period; institutions refer to SS 35 "Zakah", regulatory requirements, or their Shari'ah supervisory board (Scope).
Standard excludes Zakah on agricultural produce and other non-annual produce; institution develops its own accounting policy and discloses reconciliation for such Zakah (Scope).
Advance Zakah defined as the amount paid over and above the recognised Zakah expense, including excess paid through adjustment to equity for current and prior years (Definitions a).
Annual Zakah base defined as the total net amount subject to Zakah at the end of an annual period, excluding agriculture or other non-annual produce (Definitions b).
Institutions not obliged to pay Zakah are those not required to pay on behalf of one or certain classes of stakeholders (Definitions c).

Institutions obliged to pay Zakah are those meeting one or more of four conditions: law/regulation requirement, constitution documents requirement, shareholders' general assembly resolution, or contractual requirement with stakeholders (Definitions d, i-iv).
Realisable value defined as the entity-specific value at which the institution is able to sell/convert the asset to cash (Definitions e).

Zakah defined as a right (a religious responsibility on a Muslim) due on certain wealth, disbursable to eight specific beneficiary categories per Al-Quran At-Tauba:60; may be an institutional expense or an individual stakeholder obligation depending on legal environment (Definitions g, fn3).

Zakatable assets, Zakah liability (unpaid current and prior years Zakah due), and Zakah rate defined, with Zakah rate per SS 35 paragraph 3/2/4 and Nisab (Zakatable wealth stratum) per SS 35 paragraph 3/2/2 (Definitions h, i, j, fn4).

Institutions obliged to pay Zakah by law or constitution documents recognise current Zakah due (or reversal) as an expense in profit or loss for the period (Recognition of current Zakah due as an expense).

Where not legally required and the institution acts as agent, Zakah paid is adjusted against the equity of relevant stakeholders; where distributable reserves are insufficient, the Zakah due is recorded as receivable from those stakeholders (Recognition of Zakah as adjustment to equity).
Current Zakah due is recognised as a liability; amounts paid in excess of the amount due for current/prior periods are recognised as advance Zakah (Recognition of Zakah liability).

Institutions not obliged to pay Zakah must disclose the Zakah base, total Zakah due on that base, and Zakah per share/unit for the current period for applicable stakeholders (Institutions not obliged to pay Zakah).

Minimum disclosure requirements (a-l) include: method for determining the Zakah base and its reconciliation; authoritative guidance used; Zakah per share/unit per pool; reconciliation of Zakah liability/expense between consolidated and subsidiaries' separate financial statements; statement on whether the institution collects/pays Zakah for participatory stakeholders; disclosure where a single recipient receives more than 5% of total Zakah payable; difference between legally required and voluntarily determined Zakah; amount due from participatory stakeholders' equity; and disputes with Zakah authorities (Presentation and disclosure requirements a-l).

Established Zakah liability and corresponding assets must be transferred immediately to a segregated Zakah fund, treated distinct and separate from the institution, and not available to the institution even in liquidation or bankruptcy (Zakah fund).

Where the Zakah fund is invested or kept in a current (Qard) account not with the institution itself, per a Shari'ah-board-approved policy aligned with SS 35 paragraphs 2/2 and 10/4, the institution must disclose the amounts, returns earned, and reasons for any delayed Zakah payment (Zakah fund, fn5).
Standard is effective for financial periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023, with early adoption permitted (Effective date).
Standard supersedes FAS 9 "Zakah" (PR4; Amendments to other standards).

Appendix B(i)/(ii) illustrate Zakah valuation bases by asset class: cash/cash equivalents at realisable value; receivables at par value less allowance for credit losses; Mudaraba/Musharaka investments preferably at realisable value of net assets subject to Zakah; Salam and Istisna'a receivables at par value; real estate for rent/own use, non-adjustable payables, and provisions treated as N/A or Nil for Zakah purposes (Appendix B(i), B(ii)).

Appendix C illustrates sources and uses of the Zakah fund, listing the eight Zakah disbursement categories (poor, needy, heart-winning of non-Muslims, freeing of slaves, travellers, trustees of Zakah, heavily indebted, cause of Allah) plus administration and general expenses (Appendix C).
Creditors, including current account depositors, are not considered participatory stakeholders for purposes of this standard, so Zakah on their balances is out of scope (BC12).

FAS 9 "Zakah" provided two Zakah base determination methods (net assets and net invested funds), while SS 35 "Zakah" provides only the net assets method; the standard aligns illustrative disclosure requirements with the net assets method only, without disallowing the net invested funds method (BC13-BC14).

Standard was approved unanimously at the 26th AAOIFI Accounting Board meeting held 28-29 Rabi' II 1443H, corresponding to 3-4 December 2021, and issued 27 Jumada I 1443H, corresponding to 31 December 2021 (Appendix A; H16).

standards.applicability: Applies to all conventional financial institutions providing Islamic financial services through an Islamic finance window (including a virtual window), provided the institution opts to apply the standard in its entirety (para 2, see paras 5-7); excludes: (a) a conventional institution proclaiming Islamic services without dedicated Shari'ah compliant liabilities, quasi-equity and/or equity allocated against identified Shari'ah compliant assets (para 3(a)); (b) an institution merely managing Shari'ah compliant investment funds without constituting a window, which instead follows FAS 14 'Investment Funds' (para 3(b)); (c) an SPV or virtual Sukuk entity subject to FAS 34 'Financial Reporting for Sukuk-holders' (para 3(c)).
standards.structure: Preface (p.3); Introduction - Overview (IN1-IN2), Rationale for issuing this standard (IN3-IN6), Significant changes from previous standard (IN7 a-i); Objective of the standard (para 1); Scope (paras 2-3); Definitions (para 4 a-c); Financial reporting requirements for Islamic finance windows - Financial reporting model for Islamic finance windows (paras 5-7), Selection and application of accounting policies (paras 8-9); Presentation and disclosures requirements (para 10 a-h); Presentation of summarised financial information (para 11 a-g); Effective date (para 12); Amendments to other standards (para 13); Appendix A: Adoption of the standard (board approval, working group, executive team); Appendix B: Basis for conclusions (defining an Islamic finance window and scope; financial reporting model; reclassifications on consolidation; governance structure); Appendix C: Brief history of the preparation of the standard (H1-H12).
key_points: Standard establishes financial reporting requirements for Islamic financial services offered by conventional financial institutions through Islamic finance windows (para 1).
Applies to conventional financial institutions offering Islamic financial services through an Islamic finance window, only where the institution opts to apply the standard in its entirety (para 2).

Not applicable to a conventional institution proclaiming to offer Islamic services without dedicated Shari'ah compliant liabilities, quasi-equity and/or equity allocated against identified Shari'ah compliant assets (para 3(a)).
Not applicable where an institution merely manages Shari'ah compliant investment funds without constituting a window; such funds instead follow FAS 14 'Investment Funds' (para 3(b)).
Not applicable to a special purpose vehicle (SPV) or virtual Sukuk entity, which is subject to FAS 34 'Financial Reporting for Sukuk-holders' (para 3(c)).
'Conventional financial institution' is defined as an institution with no explicit statement, by license or constitution, to comply with Shari'ah principles and rules in entirety (para 4(a)).

'Islamic finance window' is defined as a reporting entity comprising Islamic financial services offered through stand-alone branches and/or divisions; may take the form of a licensed window or a virtual window (para 4(b)).

'Shari'ah principles and rules' defined via a five-level hierarchy: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards; the jurisdiction regulator's Shari'ah regulations; rulings of the jurisdiction's central Shari'ah board; Shari'ah-related requirements of AAOIFI FASs; and approvals/rulings of the institution's own Shari'ah supervisory board (para 4(c) i-v).
A conventional financial institution with an Islamic finance window shall prepare a complete set of financial statements of the window in line with relevant AAOIFI FASs (para 5).

A summarised set of financial statements of the window may instead be presented, only on the explicit requirement of regulators, attached to the conventional institution's financial statements (para 6).

Institutions offering Islamic services without a separate branch/division must treat the group of similar Shari'ah compliant transactions and balances as a virtual Islamic finance window and apply this standard; in all cases accounting records of the window must be kept segregated from conventional operations (para 7).

Accounting policies for recognition, measurement and reporting shall be selected and applied separately from conventional operations, per the hierarchy in the AAOIFI Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting (Revised 2020) (para 8).

Materiality for accounting policy selection is determined with reference to the window's quantitative data only and the qualitative characteristics of the Islamic financial services offered (para 9(a)-(b)).

Full financial statements must follow FAS 1 (Revised 2021) and other relevant AAOIFI FASs, and must disclose the applicable governance framework, the Shari'ah governance structure, and any deviation from the standard's Shari'ah principles hierarchy (para 10(a)).

Must disclose Shari'ah non-compliant transactions, including commingling of window funds/assets with conventional operations, their movement during the period, and how such non-compliance has been or will be resolved (para 10(b)).

Must disclose how deficits in capital, solvency and accumulated losses will be covered; the number of physical branches and other channels of the window; and significant risks faced including capital adequacy and solvency (para 10(c)-(e)).

Must disclose guarantees, undertakings, pledges, charges or other non-monetary support between the window and conventional operations, and receivables/payables/placements/investments with the conventional counterpart including returns and maturity profile; notional fund transfer pricing without a Shari'ah compliant transaction is eliminated from the financial statements (para 10(f)-(g)).

Must disclose expenses and costs shared between the window and conventional operations, nature of material items, and basis of allocation, e.g., a management agreement, service contract or cost sharing agreement (para 10(h)).

Summarised financial statements must include primary statements and selected notes with minimum disclosures, an explicit statement confirming the standard was followed in its entirety, and the window's legal and regulatory/licensing status (para 11(a)-(b)).

Summarised statements must disclose Shari'ah non-compliant income/expenses and their treatment; sources and application of charity funds per FAS 1 paras 60-62; significant accounting policies where different from the conventional institution's; related party transactions including Shari'ah supervisory board members; and Zakah applicable on quasi-equity per FAS 39 'Financial Reporting for Zakah' (para 11(c)-(g)).
Effective date: periods beginning on or after 01 January 2024; early adoption is permitted, subject to simultaneous adoption of FAS 1 (Revised 2021) (para 12).
This standard supersedes FAS 18 'Islamic Financial Services Offered by Conventional Financial Institutions' (para 13).
The standard was presented and unanimously approved at the 26th AAOIFI Accounting Board meeting held 28-29 Rabi' II 1443H, corresponding to 3-4 December 2021 (Appendix A).

The standard was issued on 27 Jumada I 1443H, corresponding to 31 December 2021, following review for Shari'ah conformity by the committee of the Shari'ah board on 24 Jumada I 1443H, corresponding to 28 December 2021 (H11-H12).

standards.title: AAOIFI Accounting Board (AAB) Statement 1/2026 — Financial Accounting Standard (FAS) 40 “Financial Reporting for Islamic Finance Windows”: Scope Clarification
standards.effective_date: immediately upon issuance (Effective date section; fn 5)

AAOIFI Governance Standard (GS) 23 "Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles on Islamic Finance Windows" (exposure draft stage)
standards.applicability: Applies to conventional financial institutions (CFIs) that offer limited-scope Islamic financial services or execute certain Islamic finance transactions without an official Islamic finance window license or via a virtual window (a), and to CFIs initiating Shari'ah-compliant products/services on a small scale not exceeding 5% of total assets or net profit for a maximum of five years, in test-phase or normal business without public marketing (b); exclusion is conditional on management assessment, auditor and Shari'ah supervisory board concurrence, and RSA approval where applicable (fn 3).
standards.structure: Preface (context/footnotes 1-2 on related GS 23 exposure draft); Objective of the statement; Statement of scope clarification — exclusion (a) unlicensed/virtual Islamic finance windows with sub-scenarios (a)(i) structuring/advising Shari'ah-compliant transactions, (a)(ii) limited transactions to selected existing customers without public marketing, plus Explanation note; exclusion (b) small-scale initiation (≤5% assets/net profit, ≤5 years) with sub-scenarios (b)(i) test-phase, (b)(ii) normal course without public marketing of investment accounts; Effect of scope clarification on other standards; Effective date; Appendices — Appendix A: Adoption of the statement (Members of the board, Reservation, Executive team).
key_points: Objective is to clarify and conditionally exclude certain Islamic finance windows from the scope of FAS 40 (Objective of the statement).

AAB decided that, notwithstanding the generality of the Islamic finance window definition in paragraph 4(b) of FAS 40, certain arrangements may not be considered an Islamic finance window in the specific context of the standard (a).

Exclusion (a): CFIs offering limited-scope Islamic financial services or executing certain Islamic finance transactions without an official Islamic finance window license, or creating a virtual Islamic finance window — though such practices are not legitimised, encouraged or endorsed by AAOIFI (a).

Scenario (a)(i): a CFI involved in structuring and advising Shari'ah-compliant transactions, e.g. investment advisory, Sukuk structuring and syndicated financing, including investing in a Shari'ah-compliant tranche of the same (a)(i).

Scenario (a)(ii): a CFI providing limited Shari'ah-compliant transactions to selected existing customer(s) without generally marketing or claiming to offer Shari'ah-compliant products and services (a)(ii).
Exclusion (b): CFIs initiating Shari'ah-compliant products and services on a small scale, i.e. not exceeding 5% of the total assets or net profit of the CFI, for a maximum period of five years (b).
Scenario (b)(i): the small-scale initiation is in a test-phase (b)(i).
Scenario (b)(ii): the small-scale initiation is in the normal course of business, provided there is no public marketing of such products and services, in particular investment accounts (b)(ii).
Explanation note: while exercising these scope exclusions, a CFI shall follow the minimum requirements of Shari'ah principles and rules (Explanation).

Exercise of the scope-exclusion option depends on the assessment of management and the concurrence of auditors and the Shari'ah supervisory board, plus approval of the relevant regulatory and supervisory authority (RSA) where applicable (fn 3).

Effect on other standards: the requirements of the relevant AAOIFI FASs shall be read in conjunction with the scope clarification provided in this statement (Effect of scope clarification on other standards).
The relevant FASs referenced are particularly FAS 40 and other relevant AAOIFI FASs (fn 4).
Effective date: this statement shall be effective immediately (Effective date).
The board approved the statement at its 46th meeting held 24 Dhul Hijjah 1447 AH, corresponding to 10 June 2026, and it was issued on 15 Muharram 1448 AH, corresponding to 30 June 2026 (fn 5).
Appendix A confirms the statement was presented for approval at AAB meeting No. 46 held 24 Dhul Hijjah 1447 AH, corresponding to 10 June 2026, and was duly approved (Appendix A).
Reservation: the statement was approved unanimously by the board (Reservation).

The proposed AAOIFI Governance Standard (GS) 23 "Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles on Islamic Finance Windows", at exposure draft stage, took a similar scoping approach for Islamic finance windows and received similar public-consultation feedback (fn 1).
A similar pragmatic approach was taken by the AAOIFI Governance and Ethics Board (AGEB) while finalising GS 23 (fn 2).

key_points: Objective: sets out the principles for interim financial reporting for all institutions having adopted AAOIFI FAS, to be read with other AAOIFI FASs and generally accepted accounting principles applicable in relevant jurisdictions (para 1).

Scope: applies to institutions that have adopted AAOIFI FASs and are required to prepare and publish interim financial reports under applicable law, regulator directions and/or stock exchange requirements (para 2).
Scope: also applies to institutions voluntarily electing to prepare and publish interim financial reports (para 3).
Definition: 'Interim period' is a financial reporting period shorter than a full financial year (para 4a).

Definition: 'Interim financial report' is a report for an interim period containing either a complete set of interim financial statements per FAS 1, or a set of condensed interim financial statements per this standard (para 4b).

An institution shall take guidance from generally accepted accounting principles applicable in the relevant jurisdiction for preparing interim financial reports, unless this standard states a contrary requirement (para 5).
The institution has a choice to prepare interim reports as a complete set per paragraph 4(b)(i) or as condensed interim statements per paragraph 4(b)(ii) (para 6).
Where condensed interim financial reports (paragraph 4(b)(ii)) are chosen, they must be prepared in line with paragraphs 12-14 of this standard (para 7).
An institution shall apply the same accounting policies applied to the previous annual financial statements prepared according to FAS 1 (para 8).

Any change in accounting policy, including one resulting from adoption of a new AAOIFI FAS, follows the policy-selection hierarchy in FAS 1 (para 165, fn 1) and is applied in the same manner as for annual financial statements (para 40, fn 2) (para 9).

Other significant considerations for interim reports include: judgments in estimates; materiality (including qualitative materiality); impairment/credit losses; PP&E acquisition and disposal including commitments; litigation settlement or significant change in outcome; correction of prior period errors; changes in business/economic circumstances affecting fair value of assets/liabilities; related party transactions; and changes in contingent liabilities and assets (para 10, a-i).

An institution adopting AAOIFI FASs for the first time shall consider the requirements of FAS 36 'First Time Adoption of AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards', including the flexibility in paragraph 22 of FAS 36 (para 11, fn 3).

A condensed interim financial report shall include, at minimum: the primary statements per relevant AAOIFI FASs (listed in Appendix B) and notes covering significant changes in accounting policies and other explanations/movements (para 12).

Condensed interim reports shall avoid repetition of previously reported information, providing updates on new significant transactions, events and circumstance changes only, but must include at minimum every heading and subtotal from the primary statements in the most recent annual financial statements (para 13).

Institutions shall specifically consider material disclosures on: quasi-equity/investment accounts (FAS 1, FAS 27, fn 4); Al-Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar (FAS 31, fn 5); off-balance-sheet assets under management including off-balance-sheet investment accounts (FAS 1, FAS 27, fn 6); profit distribution related to the above; Shari'ah non-compliant income (fn 7); charity fund (fn 8); new Shari'ah compliant products/services and related new accounting policies; and Zakah fund per FAS 39 (fn 9) (para 14, a-h).
Effective date: this standard is effective for financial statements of institutions beginning on or after 01 January 2023 (para 15).

Appendix B primary statements for Sukuk under FAS 34: for business Sukuk - statement of financial position (balance sheet) and income statement disclosing earnings per Sukuk unit; for non-business Sukuk - statement of net assets with NAV disclosure and statement of changes in net assets (Appendix B).

Appendix B primary statements for Takaful institutions under FAS 42: statement of financial position, statement of income and OCI, statement of changes in owners' equity, and statement of cash flows of the Takaful institution; plus statement of financial position and statement of financial activities of the managed Participants' Takaful Fund (PTF), separately for general and family operations, and statement of the managed Participants' Investment Fund (PIF) (Appendix B).
Until FAS 42 becomes effective, Takaful entities shall follow FAS 12 'General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Insurance Companies' (Appendix B, fn 10).

Basis for conclusions: the board decided the minimum set of primary financial statements stipulated in relevant AAOIFI FASs (fn 11) remains applicable to interim reporting, even for condensed statements, so institutions cannot omit statements reflecting the true business model of Islamic institutions by defaulting to generally accepted accounting principles (Appendix C, Primary statements required for interim reporting).

Basis for conclusions on first-time adoption: flexibility already provided in paragraph 22 of FAS 36 regarding effective date of transition, financial statements presentation and restatement of comparatives was considered appropriate, with a cross-reference created rather than new flexibility rules (Appendix C, Interim financial reporting in case of first time adoption of AAOIFI FASs).

Basis for conclusions on Zakah: since Zakah applicability is based on the lunar calendar and becomes due on a specific date, accrual of the Zakah liability over the interim period is not relevant; disclosure related to the Zakah fund is part of minimum interim disclosures, but detailed disclosures are left to management's judgment (Appendix C, Interim reporting for Zakah).
The standard was presented for approval at the 27th AAOIFI Accounting Board meeting held on 27 Sha'ban 1443H, corresponding to 30-31 March 2022, and was approved unanimously (Appendix A).

Prior to issuing this standard, AAOIFI had not issued a standard on interim financial reporting; institutions following AAOIFI FASs previously referred to generally accepted accounting principles for guidance (PR2).

key_points: This standard applies to all Takaful institutions regardless of their legal form or size, including Takaful window operations (para 2).
This standard applies to Takaful institutions when presenting consolidated financial statements and stand-alone or separate financial statements (para 3).
This standard does not apply to the structure and contents of condensed or summarised financial reports prepared for interim financial reporting (para 4).
This standard is read in conjunction with FAS 1 "Part 1: Applicable on all institutions"; in case of conflict, the provisions of this standard shall apply (para 5).

Owners' equity is defined as the residual interest in the assets after deducting all liabilities and quasi-equity, representing only the equity related to the Takaful operator/shareholders (para 6(a)).

PIF (participants'/policyholders' investment fund) is the fund managed by the Takaful institution on behalf of participants collectively to make investments and earn returns, based on Mudaraba or Al-Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar (para 6(b)).

PTF (participants'/policyholders' Takaful fund) is the fund created by/on behalf of participants to share risk, entitled to contributions and returns subject to expenses, provisions, reserves and the resultant surplus or deficit (para 6(c)).

Qard Hasan is defined as an interest-free loan; in this standard's specific context it refers to the interest-free loan extended by the Takaful operator to the PTF to temporarily finance a funding deficit in the PTF (para 6(d)).

Re-Takaful is the arrangement among Takaful institutions to devise a mechanism to avoid part of the risks their PTFs may encounter, formed via contributions from PTFs on the basis of Tabarru; the term may, in dire need and subject to Shari'ah principles, include "conventional" reinsurance with adequate disclosure (para 6(f)).

Takaful is defined (adapted from SS 26) as an arrangement among participants to handle losses via donation-based contributions, establishing a Takaful fund with independent legal/financial status managed for an agreed fee (para 6(g)).
A Takaful institution is licensed to practise Takaful business, operates under a remunerated Wakala (agency) contract, and also invests fund assets via Mudaraba or investment agency (para 6(h)).
The Takaful operator represents the residual, shareholder-owned part of the Takaful institution, excluding the PTF and PIF (para 6(i)).

A complete set of financial statements of a Takaful institution comprises eight components: statement of financial position, statement of income and OCI, statement of changes in owners' equity, statement of cash flows, statement of financial position of the managed PTF (separately for general and family Takaful), statement of financial activities of the managed PTF (separately for general and family Takaful), statement of managed PIF, and notes (para 8(a)-(h)).
Assets, liabilities, owners' equity, income and expenses of the Takaful operator shall be presented separately from those of the managed PTF or managed PIF (para 10).

The standard is effective for annual financial statements of Takaful institutions beginning on or after 01 January 2025, with early adoption permitted only if adopted alongside FAS 43 and provided FAS 1 has been (or is simultaneously) adopted (para 13).
This standard supersedes the earlier FAS 12 "General Presentation and Disclosures in the Financial Statements of Islamic Insurance Companies" (para 15).

Minimum PTF liabilities include provision for Takaful arrangements, distinguishing the remaining-coverage entitlement (including loss component) from the liability for incurred claims for benefits (para B25(a)).

Minimum PTF assets include the Takaful arrangements asset (negative balance of provision for Takaful arrangements), contributions receivable net of impairment allowance, and re-Takaful arrangements asset (para B24).
In the statement of financial activities of the managed PTF, Takaful gross margin is calculated as recognised contributions less recognised Takaful costs less re-Takaful net result (para B28(d)).
Net investment returns of the managed PTF equal income from investments less impairment expense less amortisation of deferred cost plus amortisation of deferred profit (para B28(i)).
The movement in the profit equalisation reserve (PER) and the investment risk reserve (IRR), if any, shall be disclosed (para B30).

The statement of managed PIF must disclose the operator's share in investment profits as Mudarib or its fee as investment agent, including fixed fee, variable fee, and performance incentives (para B35(e)).

Where the managed PIF is based on unrestricted Mudaraba with a right/practice of commingling with the operator's own funds, a rebuttable presumption applies that the funds are under the Takaful operator's control and shall be presented on-balance-sheet as quasi-equity rather than as an off-balance-sheet managed fund (para B39).

Extent of Shari'ah non-compliant re-insurance arrangements must be disclosed, including a summary of arrangements, justification, and Shari'ah supervisory board (SSB) approval, along with any replacement plans; Shari'ah non-compliant income and related charity fund movements are also to be disclosed (paras B32-B33, B40).
divergence_notes: Board noted only the Wakala model and Wakala-Waqf model of Takaful are accepted by AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards, stating "the Mudaraba model and cooperative model are not acceptable" (para BC9).

key_points: This standard supersedes FAS 13 "Disclosure of Bases for Determining and Allocation Surplus or Deficit in Islamic Insurance Companies", FAS 15 "Provisions and Reserves in Islamic Insurance Companies", and FAS 19 "Contributions in Islamic Insurance Companies" (paras IN4, 136).

Scope: applies to Takaful institutions (as Takaful operators) and their managed PTF/PIF for Takaful arrangements including re-Takaful issued, re-Takaful held, investment contracts issued with Takaful arrangements, and ancillary transactions; excludes guarantee contracts (unless specified as Takaful) and arrangements where the Takaful institution is itself participant/policyholder unless re-Takaful in nature (paras 2-3).

PTF (participants' Takaful fund) is the fund created by/on behalf of participants to share risk, entitled to contributions and returns subject to direct expenses, provisions and reserves, and the resultant surplus or deficit (para 4(j)).

PIF (participants' investment fund) is the fund managed by the Takaful institution on behalf of participants collectively to make investments and earn returns, based on Mudaraba or Al-Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar (para 4(i)).

Takaful residual margin (TRM) is the component of the carrying amount representing unearned surplus, or at times unrecognised net cost (re-Takaful held only), recognised as the PTF provides benefits under the Takaful arrangement (para 4(w)).
Onerous arrangement is defined as a Takaful arrangement where the unavoidable costs of meeting the obligations exceed the economic benefits expected to be received (para 4(h)).
Qard [Qard Hasan] in this standard's context refers to the interest-free loan extended by the Takaful operator to the PTF to temporarily finance the funding deficit in the PTF (para 4(l)).

The Takaful operator manages Takaful operations under a remunerated Wakala contract, acting in a fiduciary agent capacity, does not assume underwriting risks/rewards, is not entitled to PTF surplus, and is not obliged to absorb a PTF loss but may be obligated to temporarily support the PTF via Qard Hasan (paras 6-8).
The Takaful operator, PTF and PIF are distinct reporting entities, although the PTF and/or PIF are, in most cases, virtual entities (para 9).
Under the general approach, a Takaful institution recognises a Takaful arrangement at the earlier of the date a participant becomes a PTF member or the date the arrangement becomes onerous (para 29).

At initial recognition, the provision for a Takaful arrangement is measured as the total of Takaful fulfilment cash flows (gross future cash flows, deferred cost, risk adjustment for non-financial risk) plus the Takaful residual margin (para 30).

The Takaful residual margin is measured as the difference between the initially recognised Takaful fulfilment cash flows, any cash flows arising at that date, and the derecognition of any previously recognised Takaful acquisition cash flow asset/liability (para 38).

An arrangement is onerous at initial recognition if the Takaful fulfilment cash flows, previously recognised acquisition cash flows and cash flows arising at that date are, in total, a net outflow; a loss is recognised and the Takaful residual margin is set to zero (paras 39-40).

The simplified contribution allocation approach may be used if the entitlement period of each Takaful arrangement is one year or less, or if it would not produce a materially different measurement than the general approach; acquisition cash flows may be expensed if the entitlement period at initial recognition is not more than one year (paras 64, 69(a)).

Re-Takaful arrangements held are accounted for by applying Part B with references to "onerous" replaced by "net gain on initial recognition"; a re-Takaful arrangement held cannot itself be onerous (paras 75, 88).

Initial seed money paid by the Takaful operator to set up the PTF is in the nature of Hiba (gift): the operator recognises it as an expense and the PTF recognises it as PTF equity (Waqf corpus if the PTF is Waqf-based) (paras 92-94).

Takaful surplus or deficit is determined as the net surplus/deficit in the statement of financial activities of the managed PTF after due transfers to/from technical reserves; accumulated deficits and at least five-year surplus projections to compensate for them must be disclosed (paras 98, 101).

Risk reserves may be created in the PTF out of determined Takaful surplus to manage investment risk or surplus/deficit volatility, with adequate levels determined per FAS 35 "Risk Reserves" paragraphs 15-16 (paras 102-104).

The PTF recognises Qard Hasan received from the Takaful operator as a liability at par value; the Takaful operator recognises the corresponding receivable at par value, subject to periodic expected-credit-loss testing under the relevant AAOIFI FAS (footnote 10: FAS 30) (paras 110, 113, 115).

Wakala fee revenue is recognised commensurate with service delivery: immediately for services already delivered, over time for services delivered over the entitlement period, and as a provision (deduction) for probable refunds on cancelled/discontinued arrangements (para 123).

The Takaful operator recognises the Mudarib's share from PTF/PIF investment profits, and fixed/variable/performance-incentive Wakala fee, as revenue, with corresponding costs recognised by the PTF and PIF at the same time (paras 126-129).
Tax benefits or expenses (including deferred tax) pertaining to the PTF and/or PIF shall be passed on to the respective fund unless the fund is exempt from income taxes (para 133).

This standard is effective for annual financial reporting periods of the Takaful institution beginning on or after 01 January 2025, with early adoption permitted only if adopted alongside FAS 42 (para 134).
At first-time adoption, a Takaful institution shall follow one of: a full retrospective approach, a modified retrospective approach, or a fair value approach (para 135).
divergence_notes: Board decided to develop the standard on the Wakala model, noting the Wakala-Waqf model "is only a variant of the same model and hence is considered to be in compliance with the AAOIFI SSs", whereas "the Mudaraba model and the cooperative model are not considered in accordance with the AAOIFI SSs and hence are not included in this standard" (Appendix B, Applicability to different Takaful models).

The term re-Takaful "may include 'conventional' reinsurance in line with the prevailing practices of the Takaful institution in case of dire need (subject to Shari'ah principles and rules) with adequate disclosures" (para 4(n)).

key_points: Control of an asset or business exists when an institution has substantially all risks and rewards incidental to ownership, meeting two conditions: exposure/rights to variable returns and the ability to affect those returns through power (para 5).

Participatory structure is defined as a contractual investment arrangement where investors share/take profit, bear risk of loss, and hold a residual interest in the underlying assets or business (para 4b).
Quasi-equity is defined as an element of the financial statements representing participatory contributions received by an institution on a profit-sharing or participation basis (para 4c).

An asset is controlled when the institution has the present ability to direct the use of the asset and obtain economic benefits, or can prevent other parties from using it and obtaining benefits (para 6).

Control of an asset is generally obtained when the asset is acquired via consummation of a contract, the contract becomes legally binding on both parties, and the consideration (if any) is paid or becomes payable (para 7).

Control of an asset may be lost when it is sold to a counterparty; given as a gift or other form of Tabarru (e.g., waiver of rights/receivable or Hiba in sharing of profit); lost, destroyed or distributed; or ceases to provide economic benefits (e.g., technological obsolescence or legal restrictions) (para 8).

An institution originating Sukuk must determine the extent of its control over the underlying assets depending on the structure and contract governing the relationship of the Sukuk-holders, the SPV, and the institution (para 10).

Control of a business for consolidation purposes requires all three conditions: power over the business; exposure/rights to variable returns from involvement with it; and the ability to use that power to affect the amount of returns (para 11).

A rebuttable presumption of power over a business exists when the institution directly or indirectly holds more than 50% of the voting rights, or has the rights to direct the business's relevant activities (para 12).

Control may exist without majority voting rights through agreement with other shareholders or the business itself, other contractual arrangements, de facto power, potential voting rights, or a combination of these (para 13).

Only substantive voting rights are considered in assessing power: rights must be exercisable when relevant decisions are required and the holder must have the practical ability to exercise them, including current substantive and currently exercisable voting rights (para 14).
Assessment of control considers voting and other rights from investment funded by the institution itself (owners' equity and liabilities) and by quasi-equity (para 15).
Any component of a business funded by off-balance-sheet assets under management, including restricted investment accounts, is classified as non-controlling interests (para 16).

De facto power (and de facto control, if the variable returns condition is met) may exist outside paragraph 13's conditions, e.g., due to widely dispersed or significant dormant shareholding patterns, or significant voting rights held under off-balance-sheet asset management (para 17).

Control excludes situations where the institution has power over a business exercisable only in a fiduciary capacity that does not translate into variable returns for the institution itself (para 18).

Where an institution manages funds on an unrestricted Mudaraba/Musharaka basis and commingles (or has an ongoing right to commingle) them with its own funds as quasi-equity, the institution as Mudarib/working partner has both power and exposure to variable returns, and therefore controls the business or its underlying assets (para 19).

A partnership (Musharaka or Mudaraba based) generally creates joint control, whereas a principal-agent relationship (Wakala or service Ijarah) generally does not, unless other evidence of control exists from a different perspective (para 20).

Performance incentives receivable by an agent are fiduciary in nature and are not considered variable returns; the contractual/constructive right to variable returns does not give the agent control because the return is not fully variable (no loss exposure) and power is exercised on behalf of the principal (paras 21-22).

Table 1 sets out control determinations across six participatory/agency structures: URIA/PV with working-partner commingling rights (all Musharaka forms, incl. commingled accrued profits) show absolute decision-making power, profit-and-loss variable returns, and working-partner control = Yes; URIA/PV without commingling rights shows control 'based on judgment (No, as default)'; RIA/restricted Mudaraba and Al-Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar show decision-making 'as per specific guidance only' or 'in fiduciary capacity only', fee-only variable returns, and working-partner control = No (Table 1, p.10; para 20 footnote 3).

Purchase undertakings are not contracts but future commitments independent of the base contract; making one a condition of the base contract is tantamount to Shari'ah non-compliance; if execution is expected to result in a loss to the agent, a provision against the expected loss must be created (para 25a).

A Shari'ah-permissible guarantee provided in the capacity of, or by, a third party, independent of the sale/transfer contract and executed after consummation of sale (and not made a condition thereto), does not affect recognition of the sale; a provision is made to the extent of the best estimate of guaranteed losses, per FAS 38 'Wa'ad, Khiyar and Tahawwut' (para 25b, fn 5).

Management or agency arrangements executed separately from the sale/transfer contract, entailing a principal-agent relationship, do not constitute continuing involvement or control over the underlying assets, since the variable economic benefits remain vested with the principal even though the power to control exists (para 25c).
Where a Sukuk was assessed as off-balance-sheet due to lack of institutional control, it continues to be treated as off-balance-sheet for the consolidation process (para 26).
The standard is effective immediately (para 27) and takes precedence over other AAOIFI FASs with regard to the principles of control of assets and/or business specifically described herein (para 28).

key_points: Quasi-equity is defined as participatory contributions with primary equity-like characteristics (no obligation to return lost funds absent negligence/misconduct/breach) plus certain liability-like features such as maturity or a redemption put option (para 4(l)(i)-(iii)).

Scope applies to Mudaraba- and Musharaka-based investment accounts, participatory-structure Sukuk, and commingled Al-Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar investment accounts; it excludes owners' equity, managed investment funds, off-balance-sheet assets under management, and liability-based accounts e.g. Murabaha and Tawarruq (paras 2(a)-2(d), 3(a)-3(d)).
Current account (based on Qard) is defined as a non-profit-bearing, guaranteed loan repayable to the institution on demand (para 4(d)).
Investment pool is defined as a virtual entity — at times a separate reporting entity — comprising the general pool plus other specific pools created by an institution (para 4(f)).

Investment risk reserve (IRR) is amounts appropriated from participatory investors' income to cushion against credit, market and equity investment risk for residual future losses after impairment (para 4(g)).

Profit equalisation reserve (PER) is appropriated to maintain a level of return for participatory (and shareholder) stakeholders, managing rate of return risk including displaced commercial risk (para 4(k)).

On-balance-sheet classification turns on institutional control per FAS 44, judged via: returns generated by available funds, frequent fund/asset transfers with owners' equity, commingling with the institution's own investments, and refunds exceeding cash-equivalent value (para 8(a)-(d)).
Underlying assets not under the institution's control, and their corresponding instruments, are accounted for off-balance-sheet per FAS 46 (para 9).
Each investment pool must have distinct assets, liabilities (rare), revenues/gains, expenses/losses, and distinct funding sources including quasi-equity and owners' equity (para 11).

Initial recognition occurs when cash/cash equivalents are received under an enforceable contract, or funds from another contract are transferred/commingled into quasi-equity, with no other precondition; measured at fair value of consideration on the contract's effective date (paras 15-16).
An institution may hold cash/cash equivalents in the investment pool to meet regulatory (including liquidity management) requirements (para 21).
Before allocating profit to the institution as Mudarib, the pool deducts net transfers to profit equalisation/special reserves and to non-presently-distributable fair value reserves (para 25(a)-(b)).

Net profits are appropriated proportionately to funds invested by quasi-equity vs. owners' equity, then the Mudarib takes its contractual share from quasi-equity's portion; net losses are allocated proportionately to funds invested by each party (paras 26-27).
IRR set aside from unpaid/undistributed profits remains part of the investment pool until utilised or reversed to the income from which it was created (para 29).

Losses in an investment pool are absorbed first via IRR reversal, then charged to pool income, then (if inevitable) deducted proportionately from quasi-equity and owners' equity; losses from institutional misconduct/negligence are borne by the institution, not the pool (paras 31-32).

Derecognition requires the equivalent value of underlying assets to be fully determined, settled/discharged or transferred on the holder's instruction, and the underlying contract terminated with no further enforceable obligations (para 33(a)-(b)).

If a quasi-equity contract (e.g., Mudaraba) is revoked due to the institution's non-fulfilment of terms, the returned funds become a liability of the institution held on trust, valued per para 33(a) (paras 34-35).

Commingled Al-Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar funds invested in a Mudaraba-basis pool are treated as the principal's own investment (commingling does not signify institutional control); profit before the Mudarib's share is shared among all investors per SS 46 para 12/1/1 (para 36(a)-(c)).

There is a rebuttable presumption that Musharaka- and Mudaraba-structured Sukuk are quasi-equity unless they meet equity or off-balance-sheet criteria; Al-Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar Sukuk not meeting off-balance-sheet criteria are on-balance-sheet quasi-equity Sukuk if they meet the para 15 criteria (paras 39-40).

For multi-currency pools, each investment pool's currency must be identified; foreign-currency underlying assets and quasi-equity are converted to the pool's currency, with periodic translation differences attributable to the pool (paras 43-44).
Quasi-equity, including investment accounts, is presented in the statement of financial position between owners' equity and liabilities (para 45).

Required disclosures include the minimum percentage of quasi-equity agreed to be invested to produce returns, the Mudarib's profit percentage, PER and IRR ratios to the total investment pool, and different types of Hiba plus the amount/description of any incentive or Hiba (paras 48(g), 50(a), 50(i), 51(a)).

Takaful institutions' participants' investment funds (PIFs) are generally treated as off-balance-sheet managed assets since they do not meet control criteria, but may become on-balance-sheet quasi-equity in rare cases of commingling that establish control; Takaful institutions issuing participatory Sukuk must follow this standard (BC9-BC11).

Effective for financial reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, with early adoption encouraged; this standard, together with FAS 46 "Off-Balance-Sheet Assets Under Management," supersedes FAS 27 "Investment Accounts" (paras 53-54).

key_points: Objective is to establish principles of financial reporting for off-balance-sheet assets under management in line with the AAOIFI Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting (para 1).

Applies to all Islamic financial institutions managing assets in a fiduciary capacity without control; excludes participants' Takaful/investment funds of a Takaful institution and separate-legal-entity investment funds reported under other AAOIFI FAS, e.g. FAS 14 (para 2).

Fiduciary capacity is defined as the capacity to act, in good faith, on behalf of and for the benefit of another party with a duty to preserve trust; off-balance-sheet assets under management are defined as assets held, managed, administered or otherwise dealt with in an arrangement giving the institution fiduciary responsibility but not control (para 3, a-b).

Participatory investment instruments are defined as instruments (particularly including investment accounts) whereby investors share/take profit, bear risk of loss, and hold a residual interest in the underlying assets or business (an investment pool), per Shari'ah principles (para 3d).

Participatory investment instruments split into two categories: institution-controlled (classified quasi-equity) versus institution-not-controlling and managed only in a fiduciary capacity (classified off-balance-sheet) (para 4).

Off-balance-sheet classification requires all five conditions: fiduciary-only management (typically via Al-Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar, restricted Mudaraba or similar); entitlement limited to fee and/or profit share with no residual interest beyond that remuneration; absence of control per the control definition; satisfaction of the restricted-Mudaraba test; and treatment as a separate virtual reporting entity (para 5, a-e).

A Mudaraba is restricted only if the Rab-ul-Maal has reasonably restricted the Mudarib's independent decision-making, tested against: a separate asset pool without commingling with the institution's own funds/unrestricted Mudaraba; a defined investment boundary (motive, market, platform, risk appetite, assets/asset classes, liquidity profile, currency, geography, customer class); and restricted powers of replacement, transfer and/or reinvestment (para 5d, i-iii).

Off-balance-sheet assets under management are not recognised by the institution as its own or controlled assets; they are recorded, measured and derecognised within a separate virtual reporting entity (para 6).

Accounting policies for off-balance-sheet AUM must be consistent with the institution's overall AAOIFI-based policies, unless this causes an accounting mismatch or fails to reflect the business model, in which case an alternative AAOIFI-FAS-consistent policy is used (para 7).

Initial recognition of investors' managed funds occurs when cash/cash equivalents are received under a legally enforceable contract, or funds/assets are transferred to the virtual reporting entity on the contract's effective date, with no other precondition to effect; recognition is at fair value of consideration received when the contract takes effect (paras 8-9).

Underlying assets acquired are recognised on acquisition, and subsequently measured (with any related liabilities), per the accounting policies adopted for the off-balance-sheet AUM in line with the relevant AAOIFI FAS; investors' managed funds are subsequently measured to reflect residual interest in net underlying assets (paras 10-12).

Impairment, expected credit losses and write-offs attributable to underlying assets are recognised per the adopted accounting policies, the respective AAOIFI FAS, Shari'ah principles/rules, and contractual terms (para 13).

An institution may create risk reserve(s) in the virtual entity per FAS 35 "Risk Reserves"; impairment/ECL/write-offs and fair value losses on underlying assets may be set off against such reserves (paras 14-15).

Loss arising from the institution's own negligence, misconduct and/or breach of contractual terms is borne by the institution and shall not be recorded as a loss for the virtual reporting entity (para 16).

Where the institution injects its own funds (e.g., bridge financing or partial early put-option exercise), it must reassess whether the funds are: a non-return-bearing receivable/payable with proportionate ownership; an equity investment at par with other investors; or a multi-level arrangement per the respective AAOIFI FAS (para 17, a-c).

The institution may bear onerous-commitment loss exposure when the underlying asset's life exceeds the instrument's contractual term and the asset's expected reversion value is lower than its current carrying value; such loss must be recognised in a timely manner and charged to the institution's statement of income (paras 18-19).

Derecognition of investors' managed funds and underlying assets occurs when control transfers (sale, gift, or settlement), no future economic benefits are expected (expiry, surrender, destruction, full impairment), or the contract terminates with no further enforceable obligations (para 20, a-c).
Accounting policies applied to off-balance-sheet AUM, if different from the institution's own policies, must be identified and disclosed in the notes (para 21).

The institution must prepare and present a statement of changes in off-balance-sheet AUM as a primary financial statement at each period end, including requirements of the respective AAOIFI FAS (FAS 1, paras 136-139), with off-balance-sheet participatory instruments presented on a combined basis and disclosures provided by asset-type (paras 22-23; fn 11).

Required statement disclosure items: opening balance; investors' additional capital received; withdrawals/divestments/maturities; net profit/loss (revenues, expenses, fair value gains/losses, impairments/ECL net of reversals, and agency fee/Mudarib's share); transfers to/from risk reserves; profit distributions; and closing balance (para 24, a-g).

Material virtual reporting entities - net assets exceeding 10% of total equity of off-balance-sheet AUM or 5% of the institution's total equity - require individual statements or detailed note disclosure of the paras 22-24 information; where a separate financial statement is required, it follows FAS 14 or FAS 34 "Financial Reporting for Sukuk-holders" depending on asset nature (paras 25-26).

Additional required note disclosures: provision for onerous commitment on expected losses upon probable reversion of underlying assets; any recourse available to investors against potential loss; details of any ring-fencing arrangement; and details of any Hiba, gift, or waiver of fee by the institution to the virtual reporting entity (para 27, a-d).

Effective for financial periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, with early adoption encouraged, and must be adopted at the same time as FAS 45 "Quasi-Equity (Including Investment Accounts)" (para 28).
This standard, together with FAS 45 "Quasi-Equity (Including Investment Accounts)", supersedes FAS 27 "Investment Accounts" (para 29).

key_points: Standard applies to all transfers of assets between investment pools related to owners’ equity, quasi-equity and off-balance-sheet assets under management, of all institutions regardless of type or business model (Scope).
Assets transferred, for purposes of the standard, include all monetary and non-monetary assets (Scope).

‘Investment pool’ defined as distinct assets whose risks and rewards (wholly or proportionately) are attributable to funding from respective investors within owners’ equity, quasi-equity and off-balance-sheet AUM; generally a virtual entity, at times a separate reporting entity (Definitions a).

‘Monetary assets’ defined as: cash; contractual right to receive cash or another monetary asset from another party; or contractual right to exchange a monetary asset with another party (Definitions b, i-iii).

‘Non-monetary assets’ may include tangible assets (property, plant, equipment, inventory), equity instruments, Sukuk or instruments where the majority of underlying assets are tangible, and intangible assets e.g. right-of-use assets (Definitions c, i-iv).

‘Shari’ah principles and rules’ is as defined in para 11 of the AAOIFI Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting, applying a five-level hierarchy: AAOIFI Shari’ah Standards; jurisdiction regulator’s Shari’ah regulations; central Shari’ah board rulings (if any); Shari’ah-related requirements of applicable AAOIFI FASs; and the institution’s own Shari’ah supervisory board approvals (Definitions d, fn 2).

‘Tangibility requirements’ defined as institution-set requirements, in line with Shari’ah principles and rules, acceptable for transferring an asset (generally not being/including debt) from one investment pool to another (Definitions e).

Tangibility requirements must specifically observe AAOIFI Shari’ah Standard (SS) 59 ‘Sale of Debt’: a debt, directly or bundled with tangible assets (unless comprising a legal entity), may not be exchanged against cash / debt / monetary assets, per SS 59 paragraphs 8/1-8/4 read with 5/1-5/2 (fn 3).
Exchange of debt for a commodity (with spot delivery), usufruct, or services is acceptable subject to SS 59 (fn 3).
A debt transfer may instead take the form of an assignment (Hawala) rather than sale of debt, only at par value, subject to SS 7 ‘Hawala’ (fn 3).

‘Transfer of assets’ defined as transfer between investment pools (on- or off-balance-sheet) by sale, exchange, investment, clearing or other means (e.g., Hiba) under a contractual arrangement, or through reconstitution of multiple pools immediately following constructive liquidation, per Shari’ah principles and rules (Definitions f).

Institutions shall adopt and consistently apply accounting policy(ies) for transfer of assets between investment pools, considering business model, regulatory requirements and contractual arrangements with stakeholders (Adoption and consistent application of accounting policy(ies)).

General presentation and disclosure follows FAS 1 ‘General Presentation and Disclosures in the Financial Statements’ along with other applicable AAOIFI FASs (General presentation and disclosure requirements, fn 4).

Institutions must disclose accounting policies for six categories of transfer: (a) owners’ equity to/from quasi-equity; (b) owners’ equity to/from off-balance-sheet AUM; (c) within owners’ equity categories; (d) quasi-equity to/from off-balance-sheet AUM; (e) within quasi-equity categories; (f) within off-balance-sheet AUM categories (para 7, a-f).

Accounting policy disclosures must cover: bases/reasons governing transfers; tangibility requirements/restrictions; restrictions on short-term transfers with expected reversion (to avoid buy-back); restrictions and valuation approaches on monetary-asset transfers; reclassification treatment of Sukuk, shares and similar instruments on transfer; valuation bases used, with rationale if different from fair value; and mutual contractual commitments/restrictions between pool investors (Specific presentation and disclosure requirements, significant-aspects list a-g).

Institutions must disclose cumulative quantitative information: cumulative transfer amounts at net transfer value and associated gains/losses, plus the difference between net transfer value and fair value where they diverge (quantitative disclosure list a).
Disclosure required of valuation differences from transfers of assets in foreign currencies and their financial effect (quantitative disclosure list b).

Disclosure required of the nature/terms of significant transferred assets, their divisibility/separability and applicable Shari’ah principles, including significant assets proportionately divided between pools (quantitative disclosure list c).

Disclosure required of related-party asset-transfer transactions: nature of relationship, transaction type, total value at period start/end, and recognised/unrecognised financial effect, per FAS 1 paragraphs 99-103 (quantitative disclosure list d, fn 5).
Standard is effective for financial periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026; early adoption is encouraged (Effective date).
This standard supersedes the earlier FAS 21 ‘Disclosure on Transfer of Assets’ (Amendments to other standards).
Standard developed as a limited revision of FAS 21, identified during the 2018 AAOIFI FASs review and revision project and during the revision of FAS 27 ‘Investment Accounts’ (IN2).

Key changes from FAS 21: expands from disclosure-only requirements to full financial reporting principles plus general/specific disclosures; requires developed, consistently applied and disclosed accounting policies per transfer class; aligns terminology with the AAOIFI Conceptual Framework; improves presentation/disclosure in line with FAS 1; and aligns financial reporting requirements with Shari’ah requirements addressing buy-back and debt-transfer/tangibility issues (IN4, a-e).

Standard presented and approved unanimously at the 36th AAOIFI Accounting Board meeting held 12-13 Jumada II 1445H, corresponding to 25-26 December 2023, and issued on 18 Jumada II 1445H, corresponding to 31 December 2023 (Appendix A; H10-H11).

clauses: Tangibility requirements shall be developed in line with the requirements of relevant Shari’ah principles and rules, particularly, considering the requirements of AAOIFI Shari’ah Standard (SS) 59 “Sale of Debt”, whereby a debt directly or through bundling with tangible assets, unless comprising a legal entity, may not be exchanged against cash / debt / monetary assets.
