standards.applicability: Applies to promotional gifts and prizes (including loyalty programs) announced and awarded by an institution, on behalf of the owners and out of amounts attributable to owners' equity, to all or specific customers including quasi-equity and other investment accountholders (para 2). Excludes Hiba provided by the institution on behalf of owners as a profit-smoothening technique during computation of periodic profits and losses of an investment pool at constructive liquidation, which falls within the scope of FAS 45 (para 3).
standards.structure: Preface (PR1-PR2); Introduction - Overview (IN1), Rationale for issuing the standard (IN2-IN3), non-endorsement note (IN4); Objective of the standard (para 1); Scope (paras 2-3); Definition (para 4: a-c); Types of entitlement (para 5: a-c); Recognition and measurement - Promotional gifts (para 6), Promotional prizes: Initial recognition (paras 7-9), Subsequent measurement (para 10); Loyalty programs: Initial recognition (paras 11-12), Subsequent measurement (para 13); Classification and charging of expenses (paras 14-15); Presentation and disclosures (para 16: a-c); Effective date (para 17); Appendix A: Adoption of the standard - Members of the board, Reservation, Working group members, Executive team; Appendix B: Basis for conclusions - headings only (Need for a separate standard; Perceived impression of endorsement of certain market practices; Promotional gifts and prizes for the Qard-based current accountholders; Timing of recognition of expense relating to promotional prizes due over a longer period of time) - body text absent from source file; Appendix C: Brief history of the preparation of the standard (H1-H10).
key_points: Standard applies to promotional gifts and prizes (including loyalty programs) announced and awarded by an institution to all or specific customers, including quasi-equity and other investment accountholders (para 2).

Standard does not apply to Hiba provided by the institution as a profit-smoothening technique during computation of periodic profits/losses of an investment pool at constructive liquidation, covered instead by FAS 45 (para 3).

Promotional prize is defined as a monetary or non-monetary reward used to promote specific products/services or attract investments via a draw, achievement of a defined target, or both, awarded at a given point in time in future (para 4a).

Promotional gift is defined as a gift used to promote specific products/services or attract investments, awarded by an institution at its sole discretion, from time to time, to certain customers (para 4b).

Loyalty program is defined as points accumulated by customers against purchase or continued utilisation of products/services (including credit/debit card use) or for maintaining investments, exchangeable for cash, goods or services on a complementary or discounted basis at a future date (para 4c; fn 3).

Three types of entitlement: promotional gifts with instant entitlement, promotional prizes announced in advance and awarded at a future date mostly contingent on a draw or target, and loyalty programs where obligation accumulates over a period of time (para 5).
Promotional gifts: an institution shall record an expense as and when incurred (para 6).

Promotional prizes - initial recognition requires a provision when there is an existing constructive obligation (“more likely than not” that economic resources will flow out) and the obligation is reliably measurable, including cost/expected cost of in-kind prizes (para 7a-b).

A constructive obligation normally arises when an announcement is clearly communicated (explicit statements or consistent history of past actions) to a specific class of customers (e.g., investment accountholders), creating a valid expectation the institution will honour its commitment (para 8; fn 4 cross-refers para BC5).
The provision recognised for promotional prizes is charged as an expense, except where the deferred-recognition conditions of paragraph 15 apply (para 9).

Promotional prize provisions: carrying amount reviewed at the end of each financial reporting period, with changes accounted for as a change in accounting estimate and recognised as expense (or reversal), except where paragraph 15 applies (para 10).

Loyalty programs - initial recognition: provision recorded based on points accumulated, considering (where significant) probability of expected utilisation and timing of utilisation of points (para 11a-b).
The amount of provision recognised for loyalty points is charged as an expense (para 12).

Loyalty program provisions: carrying amount reviewed at the end of each financial reporting period, with changes accounted for as a change in accounting estimate and recognised as expense (or reversal) for the period (para 13).

Expenses under paragraphs 6, 9-10 and 12-13 are recognised as promotional and marketing expenses, generally charged to owners' equity, unless the scheme relates to asset-side or service-based products funded by an investment pool, in which case it is an expense of that investment pool (para 14).

Generally, promotional-prize expenses are recognised immediately; however, certain material promotional prizes not yet vested may justify recognising a corresponding asset amortised over time, subject to three conditions (para 15).

Deferred-asset condition: the promotional prize is part of a marketing/promotion campaign spanning at least 12 months, with the prize awarded at the end of, or over the span of, that period (para 15a).
Deferred-asset condition: the total obligation in respect of the promotional prize(s) must be material (para 15b).

Deferred-asset condition: a positive correlation between increased business/revenue and the asset must be demonstrated via projections/financial models, with suitability re-assessed at each financial reporting date (para 15c).

Disclosures required in addition to FAS 1: description of significant schemes; accounting policies for promotional gifts, prizes and loyalty programs; and the provision, its movement, corresponding expenses, and non-vested provisions not yet expensed (para 16a-c).
Effective date: annual financial reporting periods beginning on or after 01 January 2026; early adoption is encouraged (para 17).

The standard must be read in conjunction with AAOIFI Shari’ah Standards generally, and specifically with SS 55 “Competitions and Prizes” and relevant requirements of SS 61 “Payment Cards” (unnumbered introductory note, p.4; para 2).

The need for the standard emerged during revision of FAS 27 “Investment Accounts”; AAOIFI states it does not intend, by issuing the standard, to encourage the practice of offering promotional prizes (IN2-IN4).

The standard was deliberated and approved unanimously by the AAOIFI Accounting Board at its 39th meeting (15-16 Safar 1446H / 19-20 August 2024) and formally issued on 8 Jumada II 1446H, corresponding to 9 December 2024 (Appendix A; H8; H10).

standards.applicability: Applies to institutions preparing financial statements per AAOIFI FASs whose functional currency is the currency of a hyperinflationary economy (para 2), and to consolidated financial statements to the extent of impacts relating to subsidiary(ies) whose functional currency(ies) is that of a hyperinflationary economy(ies) (para 3); the standard shall not apply if the relevant regulatory authority does not adopt it (BC11).

Statement of income and OCI - no restatement of current period (para 22), gain/loss on remeasurement (para 23); Statement of income and attribution related to quasi-equity (para 24); Statement of cash flows - no adjustments required (para 25); Consolidated financial statements - restatement of hyperinflationary subsidiaries (para 26), non-hyperinflationary subsidiaries (para 27), differing period ends (para 28), restatement of equity-method investees (para 29); key_points: Standard establishes principles of financial reporting for AAOIFI-FAS institutions operating in hyperinflationary economies, duly considering Shari'ah principles/rules and unique business models (para 1).

Applies to institutions whose functional currency is that of a hyperinflationary economy, and to consolidated statements to the extent of impacts from subsidiaries in hyperinflationary economies (paras 2-3).
Hyperinflationary economy defined as one where money loses purchasing power at a rate that impedes meaningful comparison of financial reporting across periods (para 4).

Determination is highly subjective (no fixed criteria); indicative factors: cumulative inflation over 3 years exceeding/approaching 100% with rising trend; benchmark rates/wages/prices linked to an index; prevalent use of a stable foreign currency; prices quoted in stable foreign currency; population preference for stable foreign currency or non-monetary assets (para 5, items a-f).
An economy may be declared hyperinflationary by a multilateral institution (e.g., the IMF), respective central bank, or government, notwithstanding the para 5 factors (para 6, fn 1).
Defines fair value (incl. deemed fair value), hyperinflationary economy, index, investment pool, measuring units, monetary assets, and monetary liabilities (para 7, items a-g).

Institutions must either redetermine functional currency to a stable foreign currency where paras 5(c)/(d)/(e) factors exist and no legal/regulatory restriction applies (para 9), or apply fair value based financial reporting (para 10); historical cost basis is not appropriate in a hyperinflationary economy (para 8).
Statement of financial position items are remeasured at fair value, except items listed as exceptions (para 11).

Exceptions to fair value model: monetary assets/liabilities; assets for future delivery at pre-agreed/pre-promised value (e.g., Istisna'a work-in-progress, inventory for Murabaha, Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek); held-to-maturity investments in Sukuk and similar instruments; index-linked assets/liabilities (with or without caps/floors); and quasi-equity (para 12, items a-e; fn 5).
Exempted items are reported at carrying value, or agreement-adjusted value, or (for quasi-equity) via fair-value-adjustment effects allocated through profit/loss or reserves (para 13, items a-c).

Non-exempt items follow tiered treatment: existing fair-value items stay at fair value; cost-basis items restated to fair value via OCI as net hyperinflationary fair value gain/loss; lower-of-cost-or-NRV items to NRV; revaluation-model items revalued at least at year-end; all other items to deemed fair value via an index (para 14, items a-e).
Deemed fair value applies where fair value is impracticable due to unavailable observable data/inputs or undue cost/effort, by applying an index to the balance (paras 15-16).
FAS 30 "Impairment, Credit Losses and Onerous Commitments" applies to restated amounts, especially where deemed fair value under para 16 is used (para 17).

Deemed fair value determination (paras 15-16) may also be required at interim reporting period-ends, even where year-end fair value is normally used, if the impact within the period is material (para 18).

Index may be a general price index (or basket) or a stable-foreign-currency-based index reflecting periodic loss of purchasing power; institutions should preferably use the same index as other institutions reporting in the same economy's currency, and assess index appropriateness by asset/liability type (paras 19-21).
Current period statement of income/OCI is not restated at period end; it reflects actual revenues and expenses incurred and recognised (para 22).

Net gain or loss from remeasurement under paras 11 and 13 is recognised in OCI, either (a) accumulated as a distinct "hyperinflationary fair value reserve" categorised separately for owners' equity and quasi-equity, or (b) allocated as profit or loss for the period (para 23, items a-b).

No adjustment required to statement of income/attribution for quasi-equity beyond reflecting fair value adjustment effects on underlying assets/liabilities, via profit allocation or reserves (para 24); no adjustments required to the statement of cash flows (para 25).

Consolidated statements: subsidiaries in hyperinflationary economies must have balances restated under this standard before consolidation, translated at closing FX rates only if reporting currency differs from parent's functional currency (para 26); non-hyperinflationary subsidiaries follow FAS 1/FAS 23 (para 27, fn 6); differing period-end consolidations apply the standard to all balances at the consolidated date (para 28); equity-method investees in hyperinflationary economies are restated similarly, translated at closing rates if in a foreign currency (para 29).

When an economy ceases to be hyperinflationary, the amounts reported under this standard at the end of the last applicable period become the basis for carrying amounts in subsequent statements (para 30).

Disclosures required: hyperinflationary functional-currency status and basis applied; fair value reporting basis for current/corresponding figures plus indexed comparative figures; index identity/level/movement; net hyperinflationary fair value gain/loss for the period split (distributable/non-distributable) between quasi-equity and owners' equity; and accumulated reserve amounts attributable to quasi-equity and owners' equity (para 31, items a-e).

Hyperinflationary fair value reserve classified as recyclable to statement of income (within next 12 months; between 1-3 years; after 3 years) versus not expected to be recycled, with disclosure of expected reversal/distribution timing for quasi-equity portions (paras 32-34) and utilisation plans for non-recyclable balances, plus disclosure of any practical-necessity departures and post-period-end exchange rate/index changes (paras 35-37); accounting policy changes from applying the standard must also be disclosed (para 38).

A third column of indexed comparative figures must be presented alongside ordinary corresponding figures, computed by applying index changes from prior to current period-end for statement-of-financial-position balances, or from transaction date to current period-end for other items (paras 39-41).

Effective for financial periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, early adoption encouraged; institutions in the same hyperinflationary economy encouraged to adopt from the same date for comparability (paras 42-43); transition is on a modified retrospective basis (no restatement of corresponding figures, cumulative effects taken to opening retained earnings/reserves) from the later of the period the economy is concluded hyperinflationary or the period of first adoption, with an additional indexed comparative column still permitted and required disclosure of adjustment attribution to quasi-equity per para 31(e) (paras 44-46).
divergence_notes: Shari'ah committee deemed many generally accepted accounting principle treatments for hyperinflation incompatible with Shari'ah principles, prompting AAOIFI's out-of-the-box fair value approach rather than harmonising with GAAP (BC3-BC4).

key_points: Sets out financial reporting principles for Islamic investment institutions (IIIs), prescribing presentation, minimum contents, and recommended structure of financial statements (para 1).
Applies to all IIIs (para 2) and to employee retirement benefit funds managed by IFIs for their own employees, in addition to generally accepted accounting principles (para 3).
Excludes Sukuk-holder/originator reporting, off-balance-sheet AUM not forming a separate legal entity, Waqf institutions, and Takaful participants' investment funds from scope (para 4).
To be read in conjunction with FAS 1 Part 1 'General Presentation and Disclosures in the Financial Statements'; this standard's specific provisions prevail in case of conflict (para 5).
An III shall not consolidate, nor apply the equity method to, any entity it controls or over which it has significant influence solely for investment purposes (para 6).

Defines 15 key terms including back-end/front-end fee and premium, capital transactions, investment manager, investors, IIIs, issued value of units, NAV differential, NAV per share/unit, open-ended III, quasi-equity, Shari'ah principles and rules hierarchy, and trustee (para 7).

Quasi-equity has primary characteristics of equity (no obligation to return lost funds absent negligence/misconduct/breach of contract) combined with liability-like features such as maturity or a put option of redemption (para 7).

Rebuttable presumption that most IIIs' business model requires fair value measurement of investments, but Shari'ah-prohibited fair valuing (e.g., Murabaha receivables under FAS 28) must not be applied (para 10).
Open-ended IIIs publishing NAV per unit more frequently than the annual/interim reporting period must apply FAS 41 interim financial reporting requirements insofar as practicable (para 11).

Rebuttable presumption that units of an open-ended III always qualify as quasi-equity, requiring accounting policies for front-end fee, front-end premium, NAV differential, back-end fee, and back-end discount (para 12).
NAV differential is generally not recognised as income but forms part of quasi-equity together with the issued value of units (para 13).
Trade-date vs. settlement-date accounting policy must be developed per Shari'ah principles and rules, consistently applied and disclosed (para 14).

Investment manager fee/profit-share recognition follows FAS 31 paras 14-17 for Wakala/service Ijarah arrangements, and follows FAS 3 (Mudaraba) for profit-share arrangements, both considering variable, contingent, tiered and incentive components (para 15).

A complete set of financial statements comprises: statement of financial position/net assets; statement of financial activities/income and OCI; statement of cash flows; statement of changes in owners' equity (where applicable); statement of changes in quasi-equity (where applicable); and notes (para 18).

NAV per share/unit must be presented on the face of the statement of financial position/net assets for open-ended IIIs, with disclosure of realised/unrealised and distributable/undistributable profit or loss bifurcation (paras 20-21).
EPS/earnings-per-unit disclosure required for all IIIs except publicly traded open-ended IIIs (para 22).

Statement of changes in quasi-equity must disclose opening balances, units issued (number, front-end premium, NAV differential), units redeemed (number, back-end discount, NAV differential), net comprehensive income/loss, distributions, and closing balances, with columnar/notes presentation for multiple quasi-equity classes (paras 24-25).
Each material sub-fund must be disclosed as if it were an operating segment per FAS 1 paras 76-79 (para 30).
Investment manager and trustee are treated as related parties requiring disclosure per FAS 1 paras 101-103 (para 31).

Open-ended IIIs holding illiquid investments must disclose the proportion of such investments against total investments and the risk mitigation techniques available, including Shari'ah-compliant financing arrangements for redemptions (para 33).

Rating of the investment manager, the III, and sub-funds must be disclosed with the rating agency's name and applicable period; a Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating per AAOIFI GS 10 is noted as technically more appropriate than a conventional credit rating (para 35, fn 16).
Effective for annual financial statements of an III beginning on or after 1 January 2027, with early adoption encouraged (para 36).
IIIs with fixed maturity may continue existing accounting policies if a substantial period to maturity has elapsed and the remaining period is not more than 2 years from the reporting date (para 37).
This standard supersedes FAS 14 'Investment Funds' (PR3; para 38).

key_points: Objective: prescribes accounting/financial reporting principles for recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure of participatory ventures (para 1).

Scope: applies to accounting/financial reporting by investor(s), working partner(s), and the participatory venture itself for PVs meeting the para 4(e) definition, except exclusions in para 3 (paras 2-3).

Scope exclusions: investment accounts of Islamic banks (FAS 50), investment agency/Al-Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar (FAS 31), Shirkat-ul-Milk co-owned assets, Takaful participants' investment funds (FAS 42/43), and legal-entity investment structures incl. Sukuk except originator back-end accounting (para 3).

Participatory venture (PV) defined as a virtual, not legal, entity constituted on a Shari'ah-compliant participatory structure, including Musharaka and Mudaraba or similar structures irrespective of nomenclature (para 4(e)).
Control assessed per FAS 44 definition, resulting in three scenarios: investor-controlled, working-partner-controlled, or shared control (paras 5-7).
Investor accounting choice: pass-through approach if investor(s) solely control the PV (unless impracticable); otherwise net investment in PV approach (para 9).
Pass-through approach: investor recognises underlying assets/liabilities directly and gross in its books, proportionately if multiple investors, per relevant AAOIFI FASs (paras 10-11).
Impairment reassessed at each period end under both pass-through and net investment approaches per FAS 30, factoring settlement risk and onerous commitments (paras 12, 27).
Working partner's profit share recognised as an expense at each period end based on best estimate of amounts payable, with detailed rules for variable/contingent profit recognition (paras 15-16).
Negligence by working partner: recoverable compensation recognised as income/receivable only once negligence is established and compensation amount determined under Shari'ah principles (para 17).

Net investment in PV approach: investment initially recognised at cost (fair value if in-kind), subsequently measured at carrying amount adjusted for contributions, withdrawals, distributed profits and net profit/loss share (paras 21, 24-25).
Working partner accounting choice: off-balance-sheet approach (investor-controlled PV), quasi-equity approach (working-partner-controlled PV), or net investment approach (shared control) (para 31).

Off-balance-sheet approach: working partner does not recognise underlying assets/liabilities of an investor-controlled PV; derecognition and immediate gain/loss if it previously controlled such assets (paras 32-33).

Quasi-equity approach: working partner recognises quasi-equity equal to cash received or fair value of in-kind investment; contractually-agreed-value differences amortised over the PV term unless no fixed maturity, then recognised immediately (paras 38-40).

Perpetual PVs (no fixed maturity date and no investor redemption put option) carry a rebuttable presumption of equity classification: working partner uses quasi-equity approach as a separate equity class; investor uses net investment approach (paras 47-48).

Transfer of control from investor to working partner occurs via sale/purchase undertaking, gradual sale of ownership units, or partial redemption, recognised at consummation (offer/acceptance documentation or payment against purchase undertaking) (paras 49-50).

Gradual-transfer-of-ownership PVs (e.g., diminishing Musharaka with Shirkat-ul-Aqd) and variable-equity PVs (e.g., running Musharaka) are restricted to net investment approach for investor and quasi-equity approach for working partner (paras 58-59).

Variable-equity PV drawdowns/redemptions of quasi-equity accounted at cost (no gain/loss); profit/loss attributed per weighted average outstanding balances and contractual profit-sharing ratios each period end (paras 60-61).
Onerous commitments for redemption/gradual transfer of ownership require a provision under FAS 30 when an expected loss on redemption arises (paras 56-57).
Risk reserves accounted per contractual arrangements and FAS 35, with disclosure of balances and movements (para 63).
Summarised financial information of the PV (financial position, income/expense, explanatory material) prepared by the working partner and shared with investor(s) periodically (paras 64-66).

Effective date 1 January 2027 for institutions' financial statements beginning on/after that date, early adoption encouraged; prospective transitional application permitted with impact disclosure (paras 74-75).
Standard supersedes FAS 3 "Mudaraba Financing" and FAS 4 "Musharaka Financing" (para 76).

standards.applicability: Applies to accounting and financial reporting for deferred delivery sales (Salam and Istisna) carried out under Shari'ah principles and rules by Islamic financial institutions and other institutions following AAOIFI FASs (para 2); excludes Istisna-based development contracts, covered by pending FAS 53 (para 3); also excludes Istisna transactions where the institution as buyer intends to lease and eventually sell under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, or intends self-use/self-consumption of the subject-matter (para 4a-4b).

Appendix D: Brief history of preparation of the standard (H1-H10).
key_points: Deferred delivery sales are Shari'ah-compliant Salam or Istisna sales where the primary performance obligation is delivery of the subject-matter, excluding sales promised for a future date against a unilateral promise/undertaking to sell or purchase (para 5a).
Salam (also called Salaf) is the sale of a pre-specified commodity for deferred delivery in exchange for immediate full payment (the Salam capital) at contracting (para 5f, fn 9).
Istisna is a contract to sell a described, to-be-manufactured/acquired asset with deferred delivery, with price settled in advance, by instalments, or deferred to a specific future time (para 5b).

Parallel Salam is an independent second Salam contract the seller enters to source matching goods to fulfil the first contract, executed without dependency on the first contract's execution; sequencing of the two contracts may vary (para 5d).

Parallel Istisna is an independent second Istisna contract entered by the seller/developer to acquire matching goods, permitted only if the first buyer allows it, and executed without dependency on the first contract (para 5e).

Scope excludes Istisna-based development contracts (covered by pending FAS 53) and excludes Istisna where the buyer intends to lease-then-sell under Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek or intends self-use/self-consumption (paras 3-4).

Buyer initially recognises 'investment in Salam contract' equal to cash paid in advance; 'investment in Istisna contract' equals Istisna cost price with a contra liability 'Istisna price payable', presented net (para 6a-6b).

Buyer recognises inventory once it obtains control (substantially all risks and rewards) of the subject-matter, initially at cost including taxes, transport/handling, related Takaful costs, and agent fees, net of trade discounts/rebates/performance bonus (paras 7-8).

Buyer's investment in Salam/Istisna is subsequently carried at outstanding amount less impairment allowance per the relevant AAOIFI FAS; seller delay or inability to deliver is objective evidence of impairment (paras 10-12).

Buyer's inventory is measured after initial recognition at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV); non-conforming delivery may trigger NRV reassessment; extra handling/holding costs are expensed as incurred (paras 13-16).

Buyer derecognises investment in Salam/Istisna on complete delivery (or agreed substitute), on mutually agreed refund when goods are no longer deliverable, when unrecoverable due to seller insolvency, or when the buyer waives the right or gifts it as Hiba (para 17).

Buyer recognises revenue at gross value only when the subject-matter is sold to the eventual buyer (directly or via agent), coinciding with transfer of control; no revenue/profit before that sale; agency fee is accounted for separately, not netted against gross revenue (paras 19-20).
Goods bought under a deferred delivery sale and resold to the eventual buyer under Murabaha or another deferred-payment sale follow the revenue recognition requirements of FAS 28 (para 21).

Buyer's minimum disclosures cover accounting policies, investment in Salam/Istisna and Istisna price payable balances, related liabilities, impairment movements, NRV adjustments, receivables, deferred profit movements, credit losses, and amounts waived/written off (para 22); Salam and Istisna disclosures may be separated where material (para 23).

Seller initially recognises a liability 'Salam goods deliverable' equal to cash received, or 'Istisna goods deliverable' equal to Istisna cost price with a contra asset 'Istisna price receivable', presented net (para 25a-25b).
Seller's liability for Salam/Istisna goods deliverable is subsequently measured at its outstanding amount; onerous deferred delivery sales contracts are dealt with per FAS 30 (paras 26-27).

Seller recognises revenue at gross value only at eventual consummation of sale/transfer of control to the buyer; for Istisna with deferred payment, an appropriate proportion of profit is deferred per FAS 28 (paras 29-30).

Seller's minimum disclosures cover accounting policies, Salam/Istisna goods deliverable liabilities, Istisna price receivable, inventory classification and holding-period risk, sales revenue/cost/profit, deferred profit movements, and impairment/onerous-commitment allowances (para 31); may be separated by contract type where material (para 32).

Parallel Salam and Parallel Istisna transactions are accounted for separately as a buyer leg (paras 6-24) and a seller leg (paras 25-33) on a mutually exclusive basis, with balances presented without netting and cross-referenced (paras 24, 33-35).

Subsequent mutually-agreed changes to price or subject-matter (including Istisna performance-based price changes per a pre-agreed contractual mechanism) are not gain/loss events at the time of change; profit/loss is recognised only at eventual sale, though the event may evidence impairment or need for NRV adjustment (paras 36-37).
Standard is effective for financial periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, with early adoption encouraged (para 38).

This standard, together with FAS 53 'Istisna-Based Development Contracts' (approved by the board in principle, to be issued shortly after completion of due process), supersedes the earlier FAS 7 'Salam and Parallel Salam' and FAS 10 'Istisna'a and Parallel Istisna'a' (PR4, fn 1; para 39).

Board concluded Salam/Istisna are trade-based sale transactions, not financial instruments; profit is legitimised only once the Bay (sale) takes place, and accrual before that could be tantamount to Riba since the asset is a non-monetary debt (paras BC15-BC16).
Institutions executing deferred delivery sales are recommended to maintain profit equalisation reserves to smoothen returns to stakeholders, per FAS 35 'Risk Reserves' (para BC18).

divergence_evidence.position: AAOIFI: deferred delivery sales (Salam/Istisna) are scoped separately from unilateral-promise sales — in Salam/Istisna the sale is executed at the contract date with only delivery deferred, whereas a promise-based future sale is executed only on the future date, and the promise itself is either non-binding or binding on only one party while the other party retains the option not to execute; accounting for promises is instead covered in FAS 38 'Wa'ad, Khiyar and Tahawwut' (paras BC4-BC5, fn 22)

standards.applicability: Applicable to all financial statements prepared by Islamic insurance companies and Takaful companies (fn 1), regardless of legal form, country of incorporation, or size (para 1); if requirements conflict with a company's charter or local laws/regulations, that conflict must be disclosed (para 1).
standards.structure: Preface (unnumbered); Statement of the Standard: 1. Scope of the Standard (para 1); 2. Disclosure of Significant Accounting Policies (paras 2-5); 3. General Disclosure in the Notes to the Financial Statements (paras 6-18); 4. General Disclosure Requirements (para 19); 5. Effective Date (para 20); Adoption of the Standard (unnumbered, lists AAOIFI Board members); Appendix (A): Brief History of the Preparation of the Standard; Appendix (B): Juristic Rules Relating the Disclosure of Bases for Determining and Allocating Surplus or Deficit in Islamic Insurance Companies; Appendix (C): Reasons for the Standard; Appendix (D): Basis for Conclusions.
key_points: Standard applies to all financial statements of Islamic insurance/Takaful companies regardless of legal form, country of incorporation, or size; if it conflicts with a company's charter or local laws/regulations, that conflict must be disclosed (para 1).

Disclosure required of the party that bears general and administrative expenses, and whether it bears all or only part; if partial, the basis for determining that part and the approving body must be disclosed (para 2).

Disclosure required of the basis used to calculate items affecting policyholders' funds: pre-operations expenditures, reserves, cost of assets used in operations, claims and compensations, treatment of commissions from non-Islamic reinsurance companies, and outstanding claims retained for reinsurance companies (para 3).

Disclosure required of the cash or accrual basis used to determine policyholders' premium contributions, and the policy applied when a policyholder withdraws or defers settlement of a premium contribution (para 4).

Disclosure required of the basis applied in treating any current and/or cumulative deficit from previous financial periods, and how it will be accounted for in current and subsequent periods (para 5).

Disclosure required of the bases governing the contractual relationship between policyholders and shareholders for: management of insurance operations, investment of policyholders' funds, investment of shareholders' funds, and the body that approved these bases (para 6).

Disclosure required of the party managing insurance operations and its remuneration: a specified fee (agency basis), a share of underwriting surplus (Mudaraba basis), or remuneration on other bases (para 7).

Disclosure required of the party managing investment of policyholders' and shareholders' funds, its remuneration (percentage of investment profit under Mudaraba or specified fee under agency), and the basis for determining that remuneration (paras 8-9).
Disclosure required of the basis applied in allocating profit generated from investing policyholders' funds and shareholders' funds (para 10).

Disclosure required of whether the party managing insurance operations or investments amended its Mudarib share or management fees during the period, and the Shari'a procedures followed in implementing the amendment (para 11).

Disclosure required of deductions (percentage or amount) from the managing party's remuneration and/or expenses it bears, made as a contribution to increase the income of the fund owners or the underwriting surplus, if material (para 12).

Where the investment manager cannot place all available funds in income-producing investments, disclosure required of whether priority was given to policyholders or shareholders in allocating income-producing investments, and the basis for that priority (para 13).

Disclosure required of whether the company calculates underwriting surplus attributable to policyholders on a segregated basis per type of insurance, or by treating all types of insurance as one unit (para 14).

Disclosure required of which method the company applies to allocate underwriting surplus, and the Shari'a basis: (a) pro rata to all policyholders regardless of claims; (b) only to policyholders with no claims; (c) to policyholders after deducting claims paid; (d) between policyholders and shareholders; (e) other methods, with details disclosed (para 15).
Disclosure required of the basis used to account for underwriting surplus declared but not collected by some or all policyholders (para 16).
Disclosure required of how any undistributed underwriting surplus would be allocated if the company were liquidated (para 17).

Disclosure required of the basis applied in determining the Zakah base and its calculation, if the company meets the criteria obliging it to pay Zakah under Financial Accounting Standard No. (9): Zakah (para 18).

The general disclosure requirements of Financial Accounting Standard No. (12): General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Insurance Companies must be observed (para 19).

Standard adopted by the AAOIFI Accounting and Auditing Standards Board in meeting No. (19), 17 Safar 1421 A.H./21 May 2000 A.D.; effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1423 A.H./1 January 2002 A.D. (Adoption of the Standard; para 20).

Insurance/underwriting surplus is defined as the excess of total premium contributions paid by policyholders during the period over total indemnities paid for claims incurred during the period, net of reinsurance and after deducting expenses and changes in technical provisions (Appendix B).

Premium contributions are ruled to be amounts wholly or partially donated; the Shari'a ruling on the surplus derives from this donation characterization, and participation implies acceptance of the policy/by-law conditions on disposition of surplus (Appendix B).

Gharar (uncertainty) in Islamic insurance is forgiven in donation contracts because, according to the Maliki school of thought, Gharar does not invalidate contracts of donation; policyholders have the exclusive right to the surplus per several Fatwas, though some Fatwas permit shareholders to share in it (Appendix B).

Five methods of allocating insurance surplus are listed, with method (a) — allocation to all policyholders regardless of claims — to be followed by default when the policy/by-laws are silent (Appendix B).

Methods of covering an insurance deficit include settling it from policyholders' reserves, borrowing from shareholders' funds or others (repaid from future surpluses), asking policyholders to meet the deficit pro rata, or increasing future premium contributions pro rata; after liquidation, undistributed surplus and related reserves should be donated to charity, except for life insurance where funds may be allocated among remaining policyholders (Appendix B).
divergence_notes: "according to the Maliki school of thought Gharar does not invalidate the contracts of donations" — doctrinal position attributed to a specific school (Appendix B).

"there are some Fatwas issued by Shari'a boards that permit shareholders to share in the underwriting surplus with the policyholders" — noted as a departure from the general ruling that policyholders have exclusive right to the surplus (Appendix B).
